_README: The labelled corpus scripts/scrub-recall.py measures the name-aware leak
scanner against. It is a DEFINITION, not a corpus: every byte of real
content is fetched from git by sha at run time, so nothing sensitive is
stored here and the file stays readable.
Two labels, and both are load-bearing. A `positive` must block: the push
carries a personal name that is not a maintainer's. A `negative` must NOT
block: it is ordinary work, and a scanner that blocks it is a scanner
people switch off. Recall alone is not a score — a gate that blocks
everything scores 100% on the positives.
Case kinds:
commit    the patch of one or more real commits, exactly as push_patch
would build it for a push publishing them.
planted   the same, with a fragment appended that plants a FABRICATED
name in a realistic position. The fragment names below are
invented; none of them is a person. Planting into a real host
commit is what makes the case a needle in a real haystack
rather than a three-line toy.
A fragment's `{name}` slots are filled at run time with a full name
scrub-recall.py builds from parts, one per fragment. No name is written
down here: a name-shaped string is exactly what the scanner this file
measures blocks, and any encoding of one is still one.
The one real positive is named by sha alone. Its content is read from git
history at run time and never written down anywhere in this repository —
that is the whole reason the gate this file measures exists.

lines: it("names the speaker whose audio dropped", () => {
const h = mountStrip({ speakers: ["{name}"] });
h.dropStream("{name}");
expect(h.alarm()).toContain("{name}'s audio stopped");
test-fixture.why: the shape the real leak took: a person's name frozen into assertion strings

lines: The strip names who dropped rather than saying a stream was lost.
{name} asked for this after a call where three people were
muted for ten minutes and nobody could tell which of them it was.

mock-payload.why: sample data, where a real name is easiest to mistake for an invented one

lines: // {name} hit this on the Thursday call: the alarm fired while

const ALARM_GRACE_MS = 4_000;
code-comment.why: an incident attributed to a named person in a code comment

lines: - Roster strip now names the dropped speaker.
Reported by {name}, who sat through the whole silent call.

lines: {name}, 2026-08-19: "I could not tell whether my own audio
was the one that dropped, and I waited four minutes before asking."
That is the sentence the alarm copy now answers.
task-quote.why: a dated quoted decision — identical in shape to the maintainer quotes the prompt must keep exempting

h.dropStream("Alice");
expect(h.alarm()).toContain("Alice's audio stopped");
expect(labelFor("ada")).toBe("Ada Lovelace");
placeholders.why: conventional placeholders and a historical figure used as sample data. No address: an address is a leak by a different rule, and a case that carries one cannot say whether the NAME was what blocked it.

positives.why: the real commit that put a person's name on this public repo's main. Read from git by sha; the name is nowhere in this file.
the same content pushed as a four-commit branch. The verdict must not depend on what it travels with.
the same content beside three commits it has nothing to do with
the same fragment inside a ~110KB push — the needle-in-a-haystack half of recall, measured separately from name sensitivity

negatives.why: the control for known-with-neighbours. Blocking here means the company caused the verdict, not the name.
the host every planted case is built on, scanned with nothing planted. Without it a planted case that blocks proves nothing — the host might have been what blocked.
a dated decision quoted by name. The maintainer exemption exists for exactly this, and a recall fix must not eat it.
the same shape again — one instance is not evidence that an exemption survived
the maintainer named repeatedly in prose about his own preferences
the maintainer's name in package metadata
the fixture names a scanner must keep letting through, or every test file in the repo becomes a leak
five clean commits pushed together. A fix that reads a big push in pieces gets more chances to cry wolf, and this is where that shows up.
